content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides an empirical study of GNNs on the hidden clique problem. The authors propose residual folklore GNNs (RSFGNN) based on Maron et al., 2019 and compare it with other standard GNN architectures on this task. The findings show that the RSFGNN architecture outperforms other baselines on the hidden clique problem in dense graphs. A brief discussion on the computational complexity of different GNN architectures is also provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

Hidden clique problem is practically relevant. Experiments are sound and described clearly. Discussions on comparisons among different GNN architectures are informative from an applied machine learning perspective.

Weaknesses:
1. Since this is an empirical study, I expected to see some experiments on real world datasets for a convincing demonstration of the claims in this paper. 
2. Current experiments could be made more rigorous and informative by testing other models for data generation. 
3. Hidden clique problem is inadequately discussed in the Introduction.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and easy to follow. The GNN architectures used are well known in the field. The experimental findings are informative for the choice of GNNs to be used when hidden clique problem is encountered in practice. Due to a lack of demonstration of the applicability of claims on any real world datasets, I am not convinced that this paper would be a strong contribution.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies a practically relevant problem of finding hidden clique in a graph. Experiments on synthetic data provide insights into the choice of GNNs for this problem in practice. The paper will be considerably improved by validating their findings on a real world dataset. My initial recommendation for this paper is reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper evaluates the extent to which Graph Neural Networks can learn to identify hidden cliques in random graphs. The authors consider a supervised learning setting and test what architecture choices can benefit GNNs when facing such a problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1) A lot of the paper revolves around explaining prior work, instead of the authors' contributions, e.g. section 2.3.
2) The paper is written in an informal manner with long sentences, which makes it hard to follow.
3) The work is purely empirical and the task is quite specific, which makes it more suitable to a workshop on ML for combinatorial optimization, for instance.
4) For an empirical paper, I would expect a more extensive evaluation. That is, a larger quantity of more recent models.
5) It's hard to follow the results with heat maps and figure two for instance is so small and dark it's impossible to read.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There are typos and formal grammar is not used across the text. For instance, "hasn't" should be replaced by "has not". Furthermore, a lot of the language employed is informal, e.g. "we now even have a taxonomy". Sentences are also quite long so it makes it hard to follow. Also, please use \citep{} when the citation is not a subject in the sentence.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please, refer to the strength and weaknesses section. This paper needs a lot of work on presentation and on extending the models evaluated. Further, since there is no proposed solution, I would consider resubmitting it to a workshop instead.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This papers aims to address the Hidden Clique Problem using Graph Neural Networks. The major contribution is the approach to synthesizing the hidden clique in the random graph. The comparison of different GNNs and their variants can be considered as the other contribution.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper is a good attempt to explore different GNNs for the Hidden Clique Problem; it is good that normalization and residual connections are added and tested in this problem. 

However, this work's technique novelty is limited.
1. Synthesizing of Hiding Clique in a random graph is very straightforward. Since this papers only aims to address the Hiding Clique instead of the Maximum Clique problem, the authors "decided to not to check for such cliques", when "it is possible that a subset S' forming a clique containing all nodes of S exists." I think if this is checked elegantly, it would increase the technique depth of this work. Moreover, it is obvious that such examples would confuse the GNNs, and it is at least good to investigate the effect of these graphs.
2. The methods in this work are basically from the literature, though two components (normalization and residual connections) are investigated in the experiments. As a result, this paper reads more like a work which investigated different GNNs on the Hidden Clique Problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
See the novelty discussion in the above.

About the experiments, I think it is good to add the comparison with Maron et al. (2019), Azizian & Lelarge (2020) and Dwivedi et al. (2020) quantitatively (like an ablation study), as they are closely related to the variant proposed in this work.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work's technique novelty is limited.

content.title: Learning to solve the Hidden Clique Problem with Graph Neural Networks
content.abstract: We study data-driven methods for the hidden clique problem in random graphs. The training data is obtained by hiding a clique in the random graph, where the signal to noise ratio is tuned by choosing the size of the hidden clique and the density of the random graph. Using synthetic datasets allows us to test empirically the performance and generalization properties of various graph neural network (GNN) architectures at different levels of difficulties for the task. We compare message passing GNNs and GNNs augmented with a single quadratic operation (matrix multiplication) first introduced in \citep{maron2019fgnn}. Adding skip connections and normalization to these augmented GNNs is shown to improve their learning process and their generalization properties without any loss in time complexity. For hard instances of our hidden clique problem, they are shown to outperform message passing GNNs.
